title: He Sold Our Baby's Crib and My Late Mother's Sewing Machine for a Gaming Setup, Then Left Our Daughter in the Garage, but the Baby Monitor and a Knock at the Door Changed Everything
fb_text:
HE SOLD OUR BABY'S CRIB, HER CAR SEAT, AND MY LATE MOTHER'S SEWING MACHINE TO PAY FOR A GAMING SETUP, AND LEFT OUR FOUR-MONTH-OLD ASLEEP IN A LAUNDRY BASKET ON THE FREEZING GARAGE FLOOR. "She's a baby. She doesn't care!" he said. But the baby monitor showed me something even worse, and the next morning, someone knocked on our door...

My name is Kaitlyn Coles. After yet another exhausting double shift at a hospital in Wichita, Kansas, I got home at 12:40 a.m. and found that my four-month-old daughter's crib was gone.

So was her changing table. So were her stroller and her car seat.

Then I found Esme asleep in a plastic laundry basket on the cold concrete floor of the garage. She was wrapped in a beach towel, and a space heater was running just two feet from her.

Meanwhile, my husband, Jaxon, was inside playing video games on a brand-new computer with three monitors.

For eight months, I had picked up every extra shift I could get after Jaxon lost his job. I work as a respiratory therapist, so I know long hours and medical emergencies. Nothing prepared me for the nightmare waiting inside my own home.

We had agreed that Jaxon would take care of Esme while he looked for another job. Instead, he spent most of his days gaming, and every time I confronted him, he swore he was job hunting.

That night, the house was dark except for the colorful glow in the living room. Jaxon sat at an elaborate gaming station, wearing a headset and shouting at someone online, with three expensive monitors lighting up his face.

I hardly noticed the equipment as I headed for the nursery. All I wanted was to kiss Esme goodnight, make sure she was comfortable, and finally rest.

But when I opened her bedroom door, I froze.

The crib was gone, leaving an empty patch of floor beside the wall. The changing table was missing. When I hurried toward the front entrance, I saw that her car seat was gone too.

Panic flooded through me as I ran back to the living room.

"Jaxon! Where's Esme?"

He didn't even take off his headset. Eyes still on the screen, he just pointed at the garage door.

I rushed across the house and yanked it open.

My daughter lay in a plastic laundry basket on the bare concrete. A beach towel covered her tiny body, and a portable heater hummed dangerously close to her.

I dropped to my knees and touched her, terrified of what I might find. The side of her body nearest the heater felt frighteningly warm, and the other side was cold.

I scooped her up and checked her breathing and responsiveness. Thankfully, she seemed to be sleeping peacefully, but the terrible possibilities made my hands shake.

Holding Esme tight against my chest, I marched into the living room.

"Jaxon, what have you done?"

He finally pulled off his headset, annoyed that I'd interrupted his game.

"Relax, Kaitlyn. I sold some stuff on Marketplace. The crib, the stroller, the car seat, and that old sewing machine your mother left behind."

For several seconds, I couldn't speak.

My mother had died two years earlier, and that sewing machine was the one thing I had managed to keep of hers. Its value had nothing to do with money. It was one of my last physical connections to her.

"You sold my mother's sewing machine?"

Jaxon shrugged.

"It was junk. You never used it anyway."

My eyes drifted to the expensive computer behind him, and I finally understood where the money had gone.

"Where's the money, Jaxon?"

He gestured proudly at his three monitors and glowing gear.

"I added it to the rent money and bought a proper streaming setup. People make thousands doing this. I'm investing in our future."

My stomach knotted.

"You spent the rent money? And you sold our baby's things to buy yourself a computer?"

His face hardened.

"I'm the man of this house, Kaitlyn. I decide how we spend our money."

After eight months of covering nearly every household expense, I could hardly believe what I was hearing.

"Jaxon, you haven't earned a dollar in eight months."

His face went red.

"Don't start. I've been stuck in this house all day with a screaming baby while you're out playing nurse."

I held Esme closer and did everything I could to keep my voice steady.

"I'm not a nurse. I'm a respiratory therapist, and I'm the only reason we still have a roof over our heads."

Jaxon stood up, furious that I wouldn't back down.

"You want to know why I put her in the garage? Because she wouldn't stop crying and I couldn't hear my game. She's a baby. She doesn't care where she sleeps."

I looked down at Esme and pictured her crying alone in that dark garage while her father entertained himself inside.

"Jaxon, you put a space heater next to her. That towel could have caught fire."

He shrugged again.

"But it didn't. You're overreacting. If you don't like it, you can sleep in the garage with her."

Then he put his headset back on and turned to his computer.

I stood completely still, waiting for even the smallest sign that he cared about our daughter. Instead, he went back to his game as if leaving a four-month-old in the garage were perfectly normal.

Something inside me went quiet.

I didn't scream. I didn't throw anything. I just looked at him and said softly, "Okay."

I carried Esme into our bedroom, laid her in the middle of our bed, and built a wall of pillows around her, staying right beside her. Then I sat on the floor, opened my phone, and pulled up the baby monitor app.

When Esme was born, I had bought a camera monitor with cloud recording. It automatically saved the previous twenty-four hours of footage, though Jaxon had never paid it any attention.

He thought it was just a fancy night-light.

I began going through the afternoon recordings, hoping to learn exactly what had happened while I was at work.

At 2:15 p.m., the camera showed a man and a woman entering the nursery and carrying out Esme's crib.

At 3:02 p.m., Jaxon appeared holding our daughter. He set her in the plastic laundry basket and carried her out of the nursery.

Then I reached the footage from 3:10 p.m.

Jaxon grabbed his keys and walked out the front door.

I kept watching, sure he would be back in a few minutes.

He never came back.

I skipped ahead, checking the timestamps again and again as my anxiety grew. Minutes turned into hours, and my husband was nowhere to be seen.

Finally, at 6:31 p.m., Jaxon appeared again.

I stared at the screen and worked out exactly how much time had passed.

Three hours and twenty-one minutes.

My husband had left our four-month-old daughter alone in the garage for three hours and twenty-one minutes, with a space heater running beside her, while he drove across town to pick up his gaming computer.

For more than three hours, nobody had been there to feed Esme, comfort her, or help her if she stopped breathing. If the heater had tipped over or the towel had caught fire, there would have been no one to protect her.

I replayed the footage, desperately hoping I had missed something. But the timestamps showed exactly what had happened.

I downloaded every important recording and made a second copy of each clip. Whatever came next, I wanted undeniable proof of how Jaxon had treated our daughter.

I didn't sleep that night.

I stayed beside Esme, listening to her breathe and watching her little chest rise and fall. Whenever she stirred, I checked on her, shaken by how close I might have come to losing her.

At 7:05 the next morning, someone knocked on our front door.

Jaxon was still asleep on the living room couch, surrounded by the expensive equipment he'd bought with our rent money and the sale of our belongings.

I picked up Esme and went to answer.

A woman in her fifties stood outside, looking serious and visibly uncomfortable. A minivan was parked behind her, and through its rear window I saw two familiar objects that made me catch my breath.

Esme's crib.

And my mother's sewing machine.

"Are you Kaitlyn Coles?" the woman asked quietly.

"Yes. Who are you?"

"My name is Lenora Prentice. I bought these items from your husband yesterday."

I looked at the minivan, unable to understand why she had brought them back. Lenora glanced over my shoulder and spotted Jaxon sleeping on the couch in front of his gaming monitors.

Then she lowered her voice.

"I came back around four o'clock yesterday to pick up the car seat. Nobody answered when I knocked, but I could hear a baby crying somewhere inside the house."

My arms tightened around Esme.

Four o'clock.

Jaxon had left at 3:10 p.m. and hadn't returned until 6:31. Lenora had been standing outside our home while my daughter was alone in the garage.

"The crying went on for a long time," she continued. "I couldn't stop thinking about it afterward."

My stomach twisted. A stranger had heard my daughter's cries while I was miles away at the hospital, completely unaware of what was happening.

Then Lenora reached into her bag and pulled out an identification badge. What she said next made me realize that the consequences of Jaxon's actions had already begun...

When Kaitlyn Coles came home from a double shift at a Wichita hospital at 12:40 a.m., her four-month-old daughter's crib was gone. So were the changing table, the stroller and the car seat.

She found little Esme asleep in a plastic laundry basket on the freezing concrete floor of the garage, wrapped in a beach towel, with a space heater running two feet away. Inside, her husband, Jaxon, sat in front of a brand-new computer with three monitors.

A Nightmare Inside Her Own Home

For eight months, Kaitlyn had worked every extra shift she could after Jaxon lost his job. As a respiratory therapist, she was used to emergencies, but nothing had prepared her for this. Jaxon had promised to care for Esme while looking for work. Instead, he gamed all day.

Kaitlyn grabbed her daughter and checked her breathing. Esme was safe, but the side nearest the heater felt alarmingly warm and the other side was cold.

"Relax," Jaxon said when she confronted him. "I sold some things on Marketplace. The crib, the stroller, the car seat, and that old sewing machine your mother left behind."

That sewing machine was the one thing Kaitlyn had kept of her mother, who died two years earlier. Jaxon called it junk. He had combined the money with the rent money to buy a streaming setup, calling it "an investment in our future."

When she asked why Esme was in the garage, he answered, "She wouldn't stop crying and I couldn't hear my game. She's a baby. She doesn't care where she sleeps." Then he put his headset back on.

Kaitlyn said only one quiet word: "Okay."

What the Baby Monitor Showed

She took Esme to their bedroom, surrounded her with pillows and opened the baby monitor app. The cloud-recording camera she had bought when Esme was born saved the last twenty-four hours of footage. Jaxon thought it was just a night-light.

  • 2:15 p.m.: a man and a woman carried Esme's crib out of the nursery.
  • 3:02 p.m.: Jaxon put Esme in the laundry basket and took her out of the nursery.
  • 3:10 p.m.: he grabbed his keys and left.
  • 6:31 p.m.: he finally returned.

Esme had been alone for three hours and twenty-one minutes, with a heater running beside her, while her father collected his gaming computer. Kaitlyn saved every clip and made a second copy of each. She did not sleep, and sat listening to her daughter breathe until morning.

The Knock at the Door

At 7:05 a.m., someone knocked. On the porch stood a woman in her fifties, and behind her a minivan holding Esme's crib and Kaitlyn's mother's sewing machine.

"My name is Lenora Prentice," she said quietly. "I bought these from your husband yesterday. I came back around four o'clock for the car seat. Nobody answered, but I could hear a baby crying inside the house. It went on for a long time, and I couldn't stop thinking about it."

Then she showed Kaitlyn her identification badge. Lenora worked for the state's child welfare office, and she had already reported what she heard. She had returned the crib and the sewing machine because she did not want to keep anything bought that way.

The Consequences

Kaitlyn handed over the recordings, and the footage left no room for doubt. When a caseworker visited later that week, Jaxon had no explanation he could defend. Kaitlyn told him to leave. With her support and the evidence she had saved, she began the legal steps to protect Esme and to separate their finances.

Esme's crib went back into the nursery, and the sewing machine took its place in Kaitlyn's bedroom, where she could see it every day. The rent was paid with help from her family and her own hard-earned shifts.

Kaitlyn says she still thinks about those three hours. But she is also grateful that a stranger listened to a crying baby and chose to act. Esme is safe, and for the first time in months, her mother can sleep without fear.
